pr_title: clock: provide k_cycle_get_64() when hardware supports a 64-bit counter
pr_body:
This change adds `k_cycle_get_64()` on platforms that support a 64-bit cycle counter.

The interface functions `arch_k_cycle_get_64()` and `sys_clock_cycle_get_64()` are also introduced.

Fixes #39934
pr_comments:
> > For platforms / drivers where there is not a 64-bit register (or a pair of lo / hi 32-bit registers), the approach I would like to take is to increment a 32-bit value when we have detected that the 32-bit counter has overflowed.
> 
> The kernel already keeps track of the uptime ticks as 64-bit integer, so `k_uptime_ticks` effectively achieves the same thing as what is described here.

Interesting. On platforms without a 64-bit counter (and in particular when a 32-bit overflow interrupt is not really available), it might make sense to simply perform some arithmetic on the 64-bit tick counter to get the "top half". E.g. 

```
// unshifted
top_half = ((k_uptime_ticks() * CONFIG_SYS_CLOCK_HW_CYCLES_PER_SEC) / SYS_CLOCK_TICKS_PER_SEC) & ~((uint64_t)UINT32_T_MAX);
```

> My concern is:
> 
> 1. Given that there are not that many hardware timers out there (especially for MCUs) that support 64-bit count register, does it make sense to define `sys_clock_cycle_get_64`?

I think it does make sense, for consistency. 

> 2. Should a timer hardware driver be responsible for emulating `sys_clock_cycle_get_64` when the hardware itself does not provide a 64-bit count register? IMO, the driver should just return something like `ENOTSUP` and the kernel should be responsible for such emulations/abstractions.

That's one option. Given that most 64-bit hardware timers will not overflow for thousands of years, a negative return value from `k_cycle_get()` could mean a failure (e.g. `-ENOTSUP`). Of course, returning an integer representative of the cycle count would also work. If it's semi-trivial to do that, then there might not be much of a down side.

> 3. Is `sys_clock_cycle_get_64` really all that useful when we have `k_uptime_ticks` that returns 64-bit uptime tick count?

If the hardware is there and it's supported, it really does make sense to take advantage of the numerical accuracy, because ticks are often not as accurate.

> Given that there are not that many hardware timers out there (especially for MCUs) that support 64-bit count register, does it make sense to define sys_clock_cycle_get_64?

From logging time perspective, it is best to have fast time stamping mechanism and hw reading may be faster than calculated sys tick. Additionally, if `sys_clock_cycle_get_64` would return negative error when not supported it could be used to setup at runtime timestamping source.

> > 3. Is `sys_clock_cycle_get_64` really all that useful when we have `k_uptime_ticks` that returns 64-bit uptime tick count?
> 
> If the hardware is there and it's supported, it really does make sense to take advantage of the numerical accuracy, because ticks are often not as accurate.

The "ticks" returned by `k_uptime_ticks` are the system timer ticks.

https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/339a6bdafbe558e3ad0ea57336e2ead62e2237ac/kernel/timeout.c#L288-L291
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/339a6bdafbe558e3ad0ea57336e2ead62e2237ac/kernel/timeout.c#L269-L277

Unless you have a buggy system timer driver that returns incorrect value from `sys_clock_elapsed`, the value of `k_uptime_ticks` and the proposed `sys_clock_cycle_get_64` here should be the same (in theory).

p.s. Looking at the documentation,

> The intent is that this counter represents the fastest cycle counter that the operating system is able to present to the user (for example, a CPU cycle counter).

It does seem that the value returned by `sys_clock_cycle_get` can be independent of the timer "ticks," although almost all system timer drivers we currently have seem to return the timer tick value.

> > > 1. Is `sys_clock_cycle_get_64` really all that useful when we have `k_uptime_ticks` that returns 64-bit uptime tick count?
> > 
> > 
> > If the hardware is there and it's supported, it really does make sense to take advantage of the numerical accuracy, because ticks are often not as accurate.
> 
> The "ticks" returned by `k_uptime_ticks` are the system timer ticks.
> 
> https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/339a6bdafbe558e3ad0ea57336e2ead62e2237ac/kernel/timeout.c#L288-L291
> 
> 
> https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/339a6bdafbe558e3ad0ea57336e2ead62e2237ac/kernel/timeout.c#L269-L277
> 
> Unless you have a buggy system timer driver that returns incorrect value from `sys_clock_elapsed`, the value of `k_uptime_ticks` and the proposed `sys_clock_cycle_get_64` here should be the same (in theory).

I have seen a number of drivers that `return 0` for `elapsed()`, and anecdotally, I've usually seen ticks as some multiple of `HW_CYCLES_PER_SEC`.

But why differentiate "ticks" and "cycles" if they are the same? FWIU, they are different concepts, hence the separate config variables.

```
CONFIG_SYS_CLOCK_EXISTS
CONFIG_SYS_CLOCK_HW_CYCLES_PER_SEC
CONFIG_SYS_CLOCK_TICKS_PER_SEC
```

> It does seem that the value returned by `sys_clock_cycle_get` can be independent of the timer "ticks," although almost all system timer drivers we currently have seem to return the timer tick value.

Perhaps it's a good time to unify those concepts.

Also, if cycles and ticks are synonymous, then we are already emulating a 64-bit counter on ***every*** system whether or not it has a 64-bit hardware counter. In that case, the current situation is somewhat at odds with @andyross' earlier change request (to not emulate a 64-bit counter).

A possible improvement would be to refactor drivers to centralize emulation of the upper 32-bits of the counter in e.g. `drivers/timer/sys_tick.c`, where there is simply a callback to increment a value when the timer driver detects 32-bit overflow.

```cpp
static uint32_t top_half;
void z_timer_cycle_32_has_overflowed(void)
{
    ++top_half;
}

uint64_t sys_clock_cycle_get_64(void)
{
    uint64_t ret = sys_clock_cycle_get_32();
    ret |= (uint64_t) top_half << 32;
    return ret;
}
```

```cpp
// int64_t for compatibility reasons
static inline int64_t k_uptime_ticks(void)
{
    return (int64_t)k_cycle_get_64();
}
```

> I have seen a number of drivers that return 0 for `elapsed()`. But really why differentiate "ticks" and "cycles" if they are the same? From what I understand, they are different concepts, hence
> 
> ```
> CONFIG_SYS_CLOCK_HW_CYCLES_PER_SEC
> CONFIG_SYS_CLOCK_TICKS_PER_SEC
> ```
> 
> > It does seem that the value returned by `sys_clock_cycle_get` can be independent of the timer "ticks," although almost all system timer drivers we currently have seem to return the timer tick value.
> 
> Perhaps it's a good time to unify that concept.

We currently have many drivers that define something called `CYCLES_PER_TICK`, which directly correlates "ticks" to "cycles"; but, according to the documentation, that does not necessarily have to be the case (e.g. "cycle" counter/timer can be a completely separate counter/timer instance from the "tick" counter/timer, that is running in a separate clock domain).

IMO, in that case, there should be two separate drivers: low frequency timer driver for "ticks" (i.e. for tickless kernel/wakeup) and high frequency timer driver for things like nanosleep.

Ideally, the whole thing should be refactored to use some form of generalised timer driver interface that can be mapped to each timer class via the `chosen` nodes in the devicetree, as we do with the rest of the drivers; but, that is something for another day.

Perhaps, someone who architected this can give us a better insight as to why it was done this way and if there is any reason not to do what I suggested above; though, my guess is that it was likely done this way because this "system timer driver" scheme predates the introduction of devicetree.
About to update with all of the changes requested, just waiting for twister..

@stephanosio That's right.  Cycles and ticks are conceptually different counters running at different rates and potentially skewed relative to each other (i.e. on the default nRF5 configuration, you will see the two clocks drift because one is a crystal and the other a counted software loop on a CPU clocked by the unsynchronized internal oscillator).

It's just the case that on most platforms you implement "cycles" as the low level counter of the same device used to implement "ticks".

Oh, and indeed the timer driver has been just a plain C API since time immemorial.  In practice it ends up being very tightly coupled to arch/soc/board level code, though.  While there are certainly some platforms that could benefit from a devicetree/pluggable setup, I don't see a lot of real value there.  Where we have had the opportunity to select timers (HPET, I'm looking at you) it's generally caused more headache than help.

issue_context.title: add k_cycle_get() that supports int64_t
issue_context.body:
**Is your enhancement proposal related to a problem? Please describe.**
Would be nice to complement `k_cycle_get_32()` and the implementation is fairly trivial on several arches. 

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Implement
```
int64_t k_cycle_get();
```

On machines with hardware support the implementation is fairly trivial.

On machines with only a 32-bit timer, there may be some easy solutions as well.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
A grim possible future where we are limited to 32-bit for all eternity.

It's not pretty.. 

**Additional context**

review_comments:
This test really only checks to ensure that the 64-bit cycle counter grows proportionately to the 32-bit cycle counter on each platform.

Ideally these tests would also check the upper 32-bits of the 64-bit cycle counter change when the 32-bit counter overflows. However, that might require some unreasonable delays added to tests which would not be great for CI.

I might add a sample application that periodically checks to ensure that the 64-bit timer has received updates to the upper 32-bits based on `CONFIG_SYS_CLOCK_HW_CYCLES_PER_SEC`.

Depending on the specific hardware configuration of a specific ARC CPU, there could be a 64-bit counter available.
We can add support for this later.
One question: if both 32-bit and 64-bit cycle counters are provided, are there any constraints or expectations on their relation? E.g. should the 32-bit one always be the least significant bits of the 64-bit one? Same frequency?
Technically speaking, the lower 32 bits do not need to be the same (but that would be ideal). They should have the same frequency at least.
I think it is best for the two to be synchronized and the lower 32 bits of the 64 bit timer should always be the same as the 32 bit timer.

Pedantry: there's no way to express that requirement in a way that is actually implementable.  This isn't a synchronization problem, you can't "lock" against the passage of time.   At best we should just specify that the two APIs should ideally be backed by the same clock, or at worst have no practically detectable offset nor rate skew.

I did not intend this to be stopping the clock between different reads... I am saying if you do the following that it will be as expected from a single timer.

1. first_read = read 64 bit timer
2. second_read = read 32 bit timer
3. third_read = read 64 bit timer

(first_read & 0xFFFFFFFF) <= second_read <= (third_read & 0xFFFFFFFF)

of course, taking into account the anomaly of rolling over.

Agreed - my main point was indeed that the requirement or expected behavior is somewhere specified and documented. I guess there are pro's and con's for both approaches, but since I would not expect both to be used and combined (comparing 32-bit one with 64 bit one or so), I'd say only have the same frequency.
